title: Implement Queue using Stacks
description: Brute force to optimized: a plain list versus two stacks with lazy transfer, achieving amortized O(1) FIFO behavior using only LIFO primitives.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue using only TWO stacks. The implemented queue should support push(x) (add to the back), pop() (remove and return the front), peek() (return the front without removing it), and empty() (check if the queue has no elements).

blocks.caption: Two stacks: one for incoming pushes, one for outgoing pops, with an occasional transfer between them that effectively reverses order twice back to FIFO

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of push/pop/peek/empty calls"],["Output","For each pop or peek call, the corresponding value; for empty, a boolean"],["Goal","Correctly simulate FIFO (queue) behavior using ONLY stack (LIFO) operations, ideally with amortized O(1) per operation"],["Constraints","1 <= x <= 9; at most 100 calls to push, pop, peek, and empty; all calls to pop and peek are valid (the queue is non-empty)"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A stack reverses order (LIFO); a queue preserves order (FIFO)","Reversing TWICE restores the original order, suggesting two stacks used in sequence"],["Both push AND pop need to remain efficient overall","Only transferring between the two stacks when strictly necessary (not on every operation) keeps the AMORTIZED cost low"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A single stack naturally reverses the order elements come out in; using TWO stacks in sequence (pushing everything from one into the other) reverses that order back again, which is exactly how FIFO behavior can be recovered using only LIFO primitives.

blocks.title: Analogy: Unloading a Stack of Plates, Then Restacking Them in Reverse
blocks.text: Imagine plates stacked one on top of another as they arrive (newest always on top, like a stack). To serve them in the ORIGINAL arrival order (oldest first, like a queue), the entire stack can be picked up one plate at a time and restacked onto a SECOND pile; this naturally flips the order, putting the oldest plate on top of the new pile, ready to be served first.

blocks.caption: Pushes always go to the "in" stack; a transfer to the "out" stack (reversing order) only happens when "out" is completely empty, letting many pops share one transfer

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: push(1), push(2), peek(), pop(), empty()

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","inStack","outStack","Result"],"rows":[["push(1)","[1]","[]","-"],["push(2)","[1,2]","[]","-"],["peek()","[]","[2,1] (transferred, reversed)","1 (outStack's top)"],["pop()","[]","[2]","1 (removed from outStack's top)"],["empty()","[]","[2]","false (outStack still has 2)"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before transferring elements between the two stacks on EVERY single operation (correct, but wasteful), notice that a transfer only needs to happen when the "out" stack is COMPLETELY empty, letting many pops share the cost of a single transfer.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A single stack naturally serves elements in REVERSE order of insertion (LIFO); pouring an entire stack's contents into a SECOND stack reverses that order AGAIN, restoring the original (FIFO) order.

Observation 2: All new pushes can simply go onto the "in" stack, without needing to touch the "out" stack at all.

Observation 3: A transfer from "in" to "out" is only NEEDED when "out" is empty (nothing left to pop/peek from); if "out" still has elements, they are ALREADY in the correct order from a previous transfer, and popping directly from "out" is immediately correct.

Observation 4: Delaying the transfer until it is strictly necessary means each individual element is moved from "in" to "out" AT MOST ONCE over its entire lifetime, even though a single transfer might move MANY elements at once.
This is the classic "two stacks simulate a queue" technique: pushes always go to "in"; pops/peeks come from "out," refilled via a full transfer from "in" only when "out" is empty.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a single plain list, always kept in the correct FIFO order directly, removing from the front on pop (accepting the O(n) cost of shifting elements).
Step by step algorithm

items: push(x) appends to the end of the list.
pop() and peek() operate on the FRONT of the list (index 0), with pop() requiring an O(n) shift to remove it.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain list naturally preserves insertion order, making peek() and pop() from the front conceptually simple.

This does not actually use "only two stacks" as the problem specifically asks; it is included here purely as a correctness baseline, since the problem's CONSTRAINT is really about which primitive operations are allowed, not about achieving a faster asymptotic complexity.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly implements FIFO behavior directly, since a plain list naturally preserves insertion order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for push, O(n) for pop (shifting all remaining elements after removing the front).
Space: O(n), for the list.

Limitation: this does not satisfy the problem's specific constraint of using ONLY stack operations (push/pop/top on a LIFO structure); the two-stack technique achieves the same FIFO behavior using only stacks, with AMORTIZED O(1) per operation.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since the problem specifically requires using only stacks, maintain two: "in" (for pushing) and "out" (for popping/peeking). Push always goes to "in." Before a pop or peek, if "out" is empty, transfer EVERYTHING from "in" to "out" (popping each from "in" and pushing it onto "out"), which reverses their order back to correct FIFO order. Then pop/peek directly from "out."

Maintain inStack and outStack. push(x): push onto inStack. A shared helper: if outStack is empty, pop everything from inStack, pushing each onto outStack (reversing order). pop(): run the helper, then pop from outStack. peek(): run the helper, then read outStack's top. empty(): both stacks are empty.
9. Optimized Solution
Use two stacks: "in" for pushes, "out" for pops/peeks, transferring only when "out" is empty.
Dry run for push(1), push(2), push(3), pop(), push(4), pop()

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: FIFO order is correctly maintained: 1, then 2, matching what a true queue would return, despite using only stack operations internally.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for push; O(1) AMORTIZED for pop and peek, since each element is transferred from "in" to "out" at most once over its lifetime.
Space: O(n), across both stacks combined.
Why This Works

Popping everything off "in" (which is in reverse-of-insertion, LIFO order) and pushing it onto "out" reverses that order a SECOND time, restoring the original FIFO insertion order on "out." As long as "out" is non-empty, its top is ALREADY the correct next element to serve, so no new transfer is needed; only once "out" is fully drained does a new transfer (of whatever has accumulated on "in" since) become necessary.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["push(x)","Always simply pushed onto \"in,\" regardless of \"out\"'s state"],["pop()/peek() when \"out\" is non-empty","Directly operates on \"out\"'s top, no transfer needed"],["pop()/peek() when \"out\" is empty","A full transfer from \"in\" to \"out\" happens first, then the operation proceeds"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The transfer check ("if out is empty") is the single key optimization: transferring on EVERY call would still be correct, but far less efficient, since it would repeatedly re-reverse elements that were already correctly ordered.
empty() must check BOTH stacks, since elements could currently be sitting in either one.

The amortized analysis relies on each element being pushed onto "in" once, then moved to "out" at most once, then popped from "out" once: three total O(1) operations per element, however many pop() calls happen to trigger the transfer.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (plain list, front removal)","O(1) push, O(n) pop","O(n)","Correct FIFO behavior, but does not use only stack primitives"],["Optimized (two stacks, lazy transfer)","O(1) push, O(1) amortized pop/peek","O(n)","Achieves FIFO behavior using ONLY stack operations, as the problem requires"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Simulating a queue with stacks relies on the fact that reversing order TWICE restores the original order; delaying the second reversal (transfer) until strictly necessary, rather than doing it on every operation, is what achieves amortized O(1) performance.
Common mistakes

items: Transferring between the two stacks on EVERY push or pop call, which is correct but loses the amortized efficiency benefit entirely.
Transferring even when "out" still has elements remaining, which would incorrectly interleave newer and older elements out of FIFO order.
Forgetting that empty() must check BOTH stacks, not just one.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Popping right after several pushes with no prior pops","A single transfer moves everything at once, correctly ordering them"],["Alternating pushes and pops","Transfers happen only when \"out\" empties, potentially multiple smaller transfers over time"],["peek() called multiple times in a row","Only the FIRST call (if \"out\" was empty) triggers a transfer; subsequent peeks reuse the same \"out\" top"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating the amortized analysis (each element moves through the system a bounded number of times total) demonstrates a complete understanding of WHY this achieves O(1) amortized time, not just that it happens to work.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Implement a QUEUE using only STACKS" (or vice versa) points directly to the two-structure, lazy-transfer technique: reversing order twice restores the original order.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you implement a STACK using only two QUEUES (the mirror problem)? A similar two-structure technique applies, though it typically requires more work per push OR per pop (rather than an amortized split), since queues do not naturally reverse order the way stacks do.

Why is the amortized complexity O(1), even though a single pop() call might trigger transferring MANY elements at once? Because each individual element is only EVER transferred once during its entire lifetime in the structure, so the TOTAL transfer work across all operations is bounded by the total number of elements, not by the number of pop() calls.

How would you implement this using only ONE stack plus recursion (an alternative technique)? Recursively pop everything off the single stack down to the bottom element, insert the new element there, then push everything back, achieving the same FIFO order using function call stack space instead of an explicit second stack.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The foundational "two stacks reverse order twice to simulate a queue" technique, a specific application of stack manipulation directly relevant to understanding queue behavior at a deeper level.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) push, O(n) pop; O(n) space.
Optimized (two stacks, lazy transfer): O(1) push, O(1) amortized pop/peek; O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Two stacks with lazy transfer, simulating a queue
Core Idea: Pushes always go to "in"; pops/peeks come from "out," refilled by a full transfer from "in" (reversing order back to FIFO) ONLY when "out" is empty
Time: O(1) push, O(1) amortized pop/peek
Space: O(n)

Most Important Observation: Reversing order TWICE (once into "in," once transferring to "out") restores the original FIFO order; delaying the transfer until strictly necessary achieves amortized efficiency
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: push -> "in"; pop/peek -> if "out" empty, dump all of "in" into "out"; then use "out"
